title: One NFA Step in a Loop
description: The inner loop of an NFA simulation: for each input symbol, take the union of transitions from every current state, then move the whole set forward.

steps.description: The script imports `traceback` so any error prints with a full stack trace.

`delta` encodes the NFA that accepts strings ending in `ab`. State `q0` loops on both `a` and `b`, has an `a`-arrow to `q1`, `q1` has a `b`-arrow to `q2`, and `q2` is the sole accepting state. `current` starts as the set containing only `q0`.

The loop walks the input string `aab` one symbol at a time. `nxt` collects the union of `delta` entries for every state in `current`. The `|=` operator adds each reachable state to `nxt`, and `current = nxt` advances the whole set.

steps.question: After the first `a`, `current` becomes `{'q0', 'q1'}`. What happens on the second `a` when both `q0` and `q1` are in the set?
steps.answer: `q0` loops to `q0` and `q1` on `a`, while `q1` has no `a`-transition. The union is again `{'q0', 'q1'}`, so the set does not grow.

steps.description: Each iteration prints the symbol read and the sorted current set. After the loop, line 13 checks whether the accepting state `q2` is in `current` and prints `accept` or `reject`.
Run it. The `delta` dictionary and the initial `current` set are created.
The loop starts with the first symbol `a`.
For the first `a`, `q0` contributes `q0` and `q1`. The union gives `current = {'q0', 'q1'}` and the print shows `read a -> ['q0', 'q1']`.
The second `a` processes both `q0` and `q1`. `q0` gives `q0` and `q1` again; `q1` gives nothing. `current` stays `{'q0', 'q1'}` and the print repeats `read a -> ['q0', 'q1']`.
The final symbol `b` processes `q0` (loops to `q0`) and `q1` (goes to `q2`). The union is `{'q0', 'q2'}`, printed as `read b -> ['q0', 'q2']`.
`q2` is in the final set, so the script prints `accept`. The NFA correctly recognizes that `aab` ends in `ab`.
